blocks.md: Suppose a policy hits some industries harder than others. Comparing affected industries before and after is not enough: everything else that changed over those years gets mixed in. Comparing affected with unaffected industries after the policy is not enough either: they may always have been different. Difference-in-differences does both: it takes the before-to-after change in the affected group and subtracts the before-to-after change in the unaffected group. Whatever hit both groups cancels out, and so does any permanent gap between them. What is left is the effect of the policy — as long as the two groups would have moved in parallel without it.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the workhorse design for policy changes that hit some units more than others, and its key assumption can be checked by looking at the years before the change.
With treated (T) and control (C) groups observed before and after a change:
In regression form, with unit and time fixed effects and a treatment intensity $D_i$ (a dummy, or a continuous measure of exposure):

**2 × 2.** Log employment in high-exposure industries goes from 10.0 to 9.7; in low-exposure industries from 10.0 to 9.9. Before-after alone says −0.3; the control group's change (−0.1) is the common trend. DiD = −0.3 − (−0.1) = **−0.2**.
**Continuous treatment.** With $\theta = -0.47$ and treatment intensity rising from 0.23 (25th percentile) to 0.40 (75th), the implied relative effect is $-0.47 \times 0.17 = -0.08$ log points.

Without treatment, treated and control outcomes would have changed by the same amount. Fixed effects remove permanent level differences ($\delta_i$) and shocks common to all units ($\delta_t$); controls interacted with $\text{Post}_t$ allow groups with different characteristics to trend differently.
Replace the single $\text{Post}_t \times D_i$ term with one interaction per year:
One year is omitted as the base. The $\theta_\tau$ before the change test parallel trends (they should be close to zero); those after trace how the effect builds.

blocks.md:
| Threat | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| Pre-trends | Treated units were already diverging; pre-period $\theta_\tau \neq 0$ |
| Coinciding shocks | Another change at the same time hits the same units (e.g. quota removal in textiles) — control for it |
| Anticipation | Units react before the official date, contaminating the "pre" period |
| Staggered timing (beyond the lecture) | With different treatment dates and changing effects, the two-way fixed-effects estimate can mis-weight comparisons; newer estimators address this |

- Reading a level difference between groups as the effect — DiD uses *changes*.
- Forgetting that a continuous-treatment $\theta$ is an effect per unit of intensity, so it must be scaled by a meaningful difference (e.g. 25th to 75th percentile).
- Calling it an aggregate effect: it identifies the effect on treated units *relative* to less-treated ones; anything that hits everyone is absorbed by $\delta_t$.

- Trade: effects of trade policy changes across industries or regions.
- Labor and public economics: minimum wages, tax reforms, any policy with differential exposure.
